Armes à distance (Ranged Weapons)3/4
Bouclier (Shield)4/6
Combat à mains nues (Unarmed)6/8

Cette répartition lui permet de développer une compétence martiale utile, tout en conservant sa spécialisation dans la discrétion et les opérations techniques.

Le choix des armes et des protections dépend de la culture et de l'histoire du personnage. Les contraintes d'encombrement, d'armure et de déplacement demeurent celles prévues par RMU.

Absence de Listes de sorts

Le Voleur ne possède aucune Liste de sorts de base professionnelle.

L'apprentissage éventuel de la magie reste soumis aux règles générales du système et aux limitations effectivement appliquées dans MERP-RMU. Les aptitudes de discrétion, de manipulation et d'infiltration ne doivent pas être considérées comme des pouvoirs surnaturels.

Le Voleur et le Roublard

La distinction mécanique demeure importante.

Le Roublard bénéficie d'une formation plus équilibrée entre les armes et les compétences de subterfuge. Le Voleur possède des coûts particulièrement favorables dans les catégories de Perception, de Subterfuge et de Technique.

Face à une serrure complexe, à un mécanisme dissimulé ou à une mission d'infiltration, le Voleur constitue donc le spécialiste naturel de la compagnie, à compétences développées comparables.

Les deux professions peuvent cependant appartenir aux mêmes cultures et exercer des activités semblables. Leur différence principale repose sur leur formation.

Bilbo Sacquet et la tradition du Cambrioleur

Bilbo constitue une référence littéraire particulièrement adaptée à cette profession, mais son histoire demeure singulière.

Il commence son voyage sans formation professionnelle de cambrioleur. Son expérience se développe au cours des aventures, tandis que l'Anneau lui donne à certaines occasions un avantage surnaturel qui ne relève pas des compétences ordinaires du Voleur.

Le Meneur peut s'inspirer de son évolution pour représenter un personnage qui découvre progressivement ses talents.

Les entreprises extraordinaires de Beren et Lúthien, notamment la récupération d'un Silmaril dans Angband, appartiennent également aux récits de Tolkien, mais ne doivent pas être ramenées directement aux mécanismes ordinaires du Voleur.

Ombre et Corruption

La profession ne possède aucune association intrinsèque avec l'Ombre.

Les actes du personnage peuvent cependant entraîner les conséquences prévues par les règles de l'Ombre et de la Corruption, notamment lorsqu'il sert volontairement des puissances corrompues, trahit ses engagements ou participe à des entreprises de domination et de cruauté.

Le vol, la discrétion et l'intrusion doivent être appréciés selon leurs circonstances et leurs intentions, sans assimiler automatiquement l'usage des compétences professionnelles à une manifestation de Corruption.

Le Voleur prend toute sa dimension dans MERP-RMU lorsque ses talents ouvrent des possibilités nouvelles à la compagnie et que les décisions qu'il prend donnent une véritable portée à son art.

Thief — or Burglar

Stealth and the Secrets Behind Locked Doors

Night has fallen over Pelargir several hours ago. In the streets descending towards the quays, the last shops have shuttered their windows, and the goods brought in during the day now rest in the warehouses. A few lanterns illuminate the routes taken by the patrols, while the crews of vessels moored along the Anduin continue their work by the light of braziers.

A young woman waits beneath the porch of an abandoned house at the end of an alley. She wears dark clothing, a short cloak and soft leather shoes. A small bag holds the tools she generally uses in her work. A knife and a neatly coiled rope hang from her belt.

Her name is Maeriel. For several years, she worked under a locksmith whose workshop stood in the merchants' quarter. Her master taught her how to make the mechanisms of strongboxes, repair damaged locks and recognise the flaws that make certain doors easy to force. Since the workshop closed, she has put this knowledge to uses her former master would probably have disapproved of.

Tonight, Maeriel must enter the offices of a merchant house.

Three days earlier, the daughter of a missing merchant came to ask for her help. Her father had entrusted a substantial shipment of timber to a business associate, but the accounts submitted to the authorities now indicate that he owed the man a considerable sum. The young woman possesses a letter describing a different agreement. She suspects the associate of falsifying the accounts and wishes to recover the original ledger before her family's property is seized.

Maeriel agreed to look into the matter. She knows the offices of the merchant house, for her former master repaired their locks some years ago. She remembers the layout of the building, the doors opening onto the courtyard and the staircase leading to the rooms where the accounts are kept.

She has spent the past two days watching the premises. The employees leave their offices after the warehouses close, but two guards remain on duty through the night. One watches the main entrance; the other patrols the courtyard and the storehouses.

The young woman waits until the city patrol disappears at the far end of the street. Then she leaves her hiding place and makes her way to a small door behind the buildings.

The lock proves more stubborn than she expected. The mechanism has been replaced since her last visit, and the rain has left moisture among its metal components. Maeriel studies the keyhole for some time, recognises the general arrangement of the bolt and sets carefully to work.

A few minutes later, the door opens.

She enters a passage cluttered with crates and stops to listen. Voices come from a neighbouring room. Two men are discussing a shipment that must be loaded before dawn. The young woman waits for them to move away, then reaches the stairs leading to the offices.

Upstairs, she finds three rooms opening onto a narrow corridor. The first contains documents of no interest to her investigation. In the second, several chests stand against the walls. The third holds a large desk, with a locked cabinet behind it.

Maeriel examines the ledgers left on the desk. Their dates correspond to the shipment she is investigating, but the accounts appear to have been copied out recently. Then, among papers kept in a drawer, she discovers a reference to a book stored in the cabinet.

The cabinet's lock is old and shows signs of wear. She manages to open it and examines the ledgers within. At last, she recognises the missing merchant's mark on the cover of a volume bound in brown leather.

She opens the book and finds the entries relating to the contract. Several figures differ from those she examined a few days earlier. She slips the ledger into her bag, intending to give it to the merchant's daughter.

At that very moment, footsteps sound on the stairs.

Maeriel closes the cabinet and conceals herself behind a hanging curtain. A guard enters the office, sets a lamp on the desk and begins checking the windows. He seems about to leave when he notices that the cabinet has been moved slightly.

He approaches it.

The young woman holds her breath. She could attempt to reach the door, but the guard stands between her and the corridor. She therefore waits motionless while he examines the cabinet. After a few moments, he shrugs and returns towards the stairs.

Maeriel remains behind the curtain for several more minutes. She hears the guard descend, exchange a few words with his companion and close a door on the ground floor.

At last, she leaves the office, retraces the passage by which she entered and returns to the alley. When she reaches her hiding place, the first light of dawn is appearing above the quays.

The following day, she will deliver the ledger to the young woman who hired her. The merchant's daughter must still convince the authorities of the value of the recovered documents. The affair could expose Maeriel to charges of breaking and entering, and she knows that an influential merchant house has the means to pursue those who have entered its offices.

But her work is done.

Since her adolescence, she has learned to study places, understand mechanisms and recognise the moments when a few precise movements can overcome an obstacle. She knows that a locked door sometimes has several weaknesses, that an experienced guard follows certain habits and that a seemingly insignificant document may disclose information of considerable importance.

She is a Thief, or a Burglar, according to the name those who meet her choose to give her.

Her true speciality lies in entering guarded places, uncovering what others seek to conceal and departing with her freedom intact.

The Art of Forbidden Passages

In the towns and settlements of Middle-earth, doors, locks and guards serve an essential purpose. They protect homes, merchandise, archives and possessions whose owners wish to keep them beyond the reach of prying eyes.

The Thief devotes their training to finding ways past these obstacles. They study mechanisms, sharpen their powers of observation and learn to move through places where their presence must remain unknown. Their art rests upon precision of movement, knowledge of human habits and the ability to recognise difficulties before they become dangerous.

This specialisation takes very different forms according to circumstances. A burglar enters a dwelling to steal a valuable object; a spy seeks documents kept in a guarded place; an adventurer examines the mechanisms protecting the entrance to an ancient chamber. The same skills may serve purposes whose moral and social consequences are profoundly different.

The character therefore belongs to a profession defined by precise techniques rather than by an activity that must necessarily be criminal. Some make their living through theft; others place their talents at the service of a patron, a community or a company of travellers.

Success seldom depends upon dexterity alone. A lock may be perfectly understood even when circumstances make it impossible to open it undisturbed. A well-hidden passage is useless if the person taking it has no idea where it leads. A mission prepared over several days can be compromised by the unexpected presence of a witness.

The Thief therefore learns to consider a situation as a whole. They study the occupants' habits, possible points of entry, obstacles that might arise and the routes by which they can depart. Their reputation often rests upon their ability to return from a difficult undertaking without provoking a confrontation.

Bilbo Baggins, the Unexpected Burglar

Among Tolkien's characters, Bilbo Baggins provides the most obvious literary reference for this profession.

When Gandalf arranges Thorin Oakenshield's expedition to Erebor, he chooses Bilbo to serve as its burglar. The decision astonishes the Dwarves and the Hobbit himself, whose life until then has unfolded in the tranquillity of the Shire.

Bilbo has received no professional training in locks, espionage or infiltration. He nevertheless possesses several qualities that prove valuable during the journey: a natural ability to move unnoticed, practical intelligence, curiosity and a growing capacity to act with composure.

His adventures allow him to develop these gifts. He learns to approach danger without being immediately discovered, to observe the habits of formidable creatures and to seek solutions when direct confrontation seems impossible.

His encounter with Smaug is one of the occasions on which his talents become particularly important. Bilbo explores the interior of the Lonely Mountain, observes the Dragon and gathers information that his companions could not have obtained in the same way.

The matter of the Arkenstone, however, lends an additional depth to his role. When Thorin refuses to negotiate with those besieging Erebor, Bilbo decides to give the stone to Bard and the Elvenking in the hope of securing an agreement and preventing a battle. In doing so, he makes a difficult choice that exposes him to the anger of the one whom he had promised to help.

The significance of this episode lies as much in his moral courage as in his ability to remain unnoticed. Bilbo uses the means at his disposal to pursue an end he believes to be right, while accepting the possible consequences of his actions.

His personal abilities must also be distinguished from the powers of the Ring he discovered during the journey. The invisibility he enjoys on certain occasions comes from an exceptional object; his effectiveness as a burglar should not be attributed entirely to that power.

Bilbo's character also reminds us that the profession can be discovered in the course of an adventure. An accomplished Burglar does not necessarily begin their story with the experience of someone who has practised the trade for many years.

Learning to Observe

Observation is one of the foundations of the Thief's training. Before approaching an obstacle, the character must learn to recognise the details that may help them or jeopardise their mission.

In a town, this knowledge concerns streets, doors, service passages and the routines of those who work there. A merchant has his warehouses opened at particular hours; a servant uses the same staircase each day; a guard sometimes changes his patrol route when he must rejoin his companions.

The young Thief learns to watch these habits without attracting attention. They discover the value of a conversation overheard in a market, a delivery made at an unusual hour or a window left open in an otherwise carefully guarded house.

Training also encompasses material details. Marks of wear around a lock may reveal that it is frequently used. A door whose wood bears fresh marks may have been repaired, while a slightly displaced flagstone might conceal a mechanism.

Awareness thus becomes an essential discipline. It allows the character to distinguish the ordinary features of an environment and recognise those that merit closer examination.

This skill does not remove the need for local knowledge. A Thief accustomed to the quays of Pelargir possesses different experience from a burglar in Bree or a spy established in Minas Tirith. Materials, architecture and customs vary from region to region.

Travel gradually broadens their eye. They learn to recognise new kinds of locks, understand the layout of unfamiliar buildings and adapt their habits to the circumstances.

Locks, Mechanisms and Traps

Knowledge of mechanisms is one of the Thief's most characteristic specialities.

Locks protect homes, chests and stores. Their design depends on the resources available, the craftsman's skills and the value of what they are meant to safeguard. Some are simple and intended for everyday use; others are intricately made and require careful examination.

The Thief learns to recognise different kinds of mechanisms, understand how they generally work and determine what means are available to open or bypass them.

This training may arise from an entirely legitimate apprenticeship. A former locksmith has valuable knowledge of locking systems. A craftsman charged with maintaining a house learns to recognise defects in doors and chests. A travelling companion sometimes acquires these skills after encountering several obstacles that required specialised work to open.

Traps call for particular caution. Some rely on simple mechanisms designed to sound an alarm or prevent intrusion. Others pose serious dangers to anyone who triggers them.

Experience teaches the Thief to look for unusual signs before touching a suspicious object. A door may be protected by several devices, while an ancient chest may retain mechanisms unlike anything the character has encountered before.

Discovering a trap and disarming it are two separate tasks. Recognising a danger makes it possible to warn one's companions; rendering it harmless may require additional skills and involve risks.

This knowledge gives the Thief an essential place in expeditions to ruins and ancient works, where opening a passage may become an undertaking as important as facing the creatures that guard it.

Vanishing Among People

Stealth is an art practised in crowded streets as well as in deserted places.

The Thief learns to move without attracting attention, use visual obstacles and recognise the moments when a watched space can be crossed. In a town, these abilities demand knowledge of social habits. Someone whose clothing and manner suit the activities of the neighbourhood may pass unnoticed more easily than a person who is plainly trying to hide.

A crowd offers certain opportunities, but also entails dangers. A sudden movement draws attention; someone coming too close to a merchant may be noticed; a guard familiar with the area can sometimes recognise strangers at once.

Concealment also concerns objects. A document must be carried without being immediately discovered, while a compromising tool may attract attention during an inspection. The Thief learns to organise their belongings and carefully prepare the movements required by a mission.

In the wild, the same qualities take a different form. Vegetation, relief and the conditions of the light become the principal means of concealment. The character must learn to recognise the noises they make and the traces they leave behind.

According to Tolkien, Hobbits possess a remarkable natural aptitude for disappearing silently when they wish to avoid the Big Folk. This ability belongs to their nature and habits, and is not in itself a magical power.

A Hobbit Thief may therefore develop this quality to a particular degree, whereas a character from another culture must rely on techniques acquired through training.

Dexterity and the Training of the Body

The Thief's physical abilities answer different demands from those of the martial professions.

Climbing, moving through confined passages and quickly overcoming certain obstacles are important parts of their training. Flexibility and precision may prove more useful than brute strength when they must reach a window, cross a rooftop or move through a cluttered space.

The young apprentice gradually develops balance and coordination. They learn to recognise surfaces strong enough to bear their weight and assess the consequences of a fall. Repeated exercises improve their speed without sacrificing precision of movement.

Moving through narrow places demands particular adaptation. An opening may appear wide enough to admit a person, but the equipment they carry may hinder their progress. Some manoeuvres require them to leave objects behind for a time or find another passage.

The ability to run and surmount obstacles also proves valuable when a mission fails to unfold as planned.

These aptitudes do not, however, protect the Thief from every danger. A serious fall or an unexpected confrontation can bring an undertaking to an abrupt end. Experience teaches them to judge their capabilities rather than rely upon agility alone.

Cities and Their Secrets

The great settlements of Middle-earth offer many opportunities to employ the Thief's skills.

In Minas Tirith, the City's successive circles, noble dwellings and administrative establishments form a setting where surveillance, rules of access and social relationships are of great importance. A character familiar with the city may know its service passages, the places where certain servants gather and the habits of influential households.

In Pelargir, the quays, warehouses and merchant houses present different opportunities. Goods circulate constantly, crews come and go, and documents relating to cargoes can have considerable value.

In Umbar, maritime activities and rivalries between powerful families may favour missions of surveillance, espionage and intrusion. The Thief's abilities become valuable when a patron wishes to obtain information without openly assuming responsibility.

In the more modest settlements of Eriador, relationships between inhabitants become more important. A stranger is quickly noticed in a small community, while a familiar face may sometimes move freely thanks to the trust of neighbours.

These differences profoundly influence the character's methods. Their effectiveness depends as much on knowledge of local society as on technical expertise.

Among the Ruins of Ancient Kingdoms

The ruins of Arnor, the abandoned works of Gondor and the ancient dwellings of the Elven peoples are places where the Thief's skills acquire particular significance.

Forgotten doors and walled-up passages sometimes conceal mechanisms whose origins go back several centuries. Some were designed to protect valuable possessions; others to control access to restricted spaces.

A Burglar accustomed to ordinary buildings must learn to recognise the materials and techniques used by craftsmen of old. The knowledge of a scholar, a Khazâd or an Alchemist can usefully complement their own.

Ruins also contain dangers unrelated to traps. Weakened floors, displaced stones and collapsed passages demand constant vigilance. A door opened perfectly may lead into a chamber whose structure is no longer safe.

The Thief brings precision, experience in observation and knowledge of mechanical devices. They help their companions explore with caution, recognise obstacles and assess the risks accompanying certain discoveries.

Within an adventuring company, these skills thus become a means of safeguarding everyone.

The Traditions of Different Peoples

The profession of Thief can take very different forms according to the character's cultural origins.

Among Hobbits, stealth, dexterity and knowledge of familiar paths offer a particularly interesting foundation. A character from the Shire may have learned to move silently through gardens, recognise the habits of the inhabitants and avoid unwelcome encounters. Choosing the life of a Burglar nevertheless remains unusual in a society where property and family reputation carry considerable weight.

Among the Dúnedain of the North, certain infiltration skills may be developed for surveillance or special missions. A character tasked with entering an enemy fortification has a different training from a Ranger, even when both share knowledge useful for moving unseen.

In Gondor, the great cities and administrative establishments offer a suitable setting for specialists in observation, mechanisms and espionage. A Thief may work for a noble house, ply their trade in the merchants' quarters or place their skills at the service of investigations.

Among Dwarves, the study of locks, doors and mechanisms may arise from a craft apprenticeship. Knowledge of stonework and metalwork gives some characters valuable abilities when examining ancient devices. The traditions of their House determine, however, how this knowledge is handed down and employed.

In Umbar and the merchant cities of the South, port activities and commercial rivalries suggest burglars, spies and specialists in intrusion. Other traditions exist among the peoples of the East and Rhovanion, according to the organisation of their communities and their local customs.

These possibilities remain subject to the cultural and chronological availability established in MERP-UI. Above all, they make it possible to create characters whose identity extends far beyond the mere practice of theft.

The Trade and Its Obligations

A Thief who lives by their skills often depends on personal relationships and agreements that may be fragile.

Some work alone, choosing their missions and carefully concealing their activities. Others belong to organised groups, where responsibilities are divided between those who gather information, those who prepare the operation and those who carry out the intrusion.

Relations with employers require particular caution. A patron may conceal an object's true destination or describe a mission as the rightful recovery of property when it actually serves their own interests.

The Thief must therefore learn to judge how far those requesting their services can be trusted. Reputation matters greatly, especially in circles where undertakings depend more upon a person's word than on legally recognised contracts.

Some characters establish rules of their own. They refuse to prey upon vulnerable people, prefer to recover stolen possessions or will not enter a dwelling until they have learned enough about the person employing them.

Others seek profit above all and regard their dexterity as a means of acquiring wealth otherwise beyond their reach.

This diversity gives the profession a particular moral depth. The character's skills enable them to cross certain physical boundaries; their convictions determine which boundaries they choose to respect in their dealings with others.

Facing Danger

The Thief possesses martial skills, but their training generally favours situations where stealth, mobility and speed allow them to retain the initiative.

They may learn to wield weapons suited to their origins and habits. Daggers, short blades, bows and thrown weapons offer useful possibilities, especially when equipment must remain light and easy to carry.

Some characters have more extensive combat experience. A former sailor, guard or adventurer who has taken part in several expeditions may have received substantial martial training.

Protective equipment must nevertheless be chosen with the intended movements in mind. Heavy armour increases the difficulty of certain manoeuvres and may compromise the stealth a mission requires.

In a prolonged fight, the Thief generally enjoys fewer advantages than a specialised Fighter. Their contribution depends more on their choice of position, their observation and their ability to intervene at the right moment.

Flight is sometimes a sensible decision. A character charged with delivering a document or opening a passage may jeopardise the whole mission by accepting an unnecessary fight.

Such prudence is fully part of their experience. The best outcome of an infiltration is often to achieve the objective without being discovered.

The Thief and the Rogue

The Thief and the Rogue share many skills, but their professional emphases remain different.

The Rogue has training balanced between weapons, mobility, social skills and subterfuge. They may become a versatile adventurer, capable of fighting, negotiating and moving through varied environments.

The Thief pursues a deeper specialisation in observation, intrusion, concealment and mechanisms. Locks and traps are especially characteristic areas of their training.

Within a company, this distinction gives both professions a place. The Rogue readily takes part in situations requiring martial and social skills to be combined, while the Thief becomes the specialist entrusted with technical obstacles and the most discreet missions.

Their personalities and motivations remain independent of this distribution. A Rogue may make a living through theft, while a Thief may use their talents in the service of a wholly legitimate cause.

Choices in the Face of the Shadow

Stealth and the ability to enter guarded places can become invaluable assets in the struggle against the Shadow. Information obtained within an enemy fortress, an intercepted message or a passage opened at the right moment may help save a community.

But the same abilities can be placed at the service of domination, cruelty or betrayal.

The history of Middle-earth preserves the memory of deeds in which entering a forbidden place takes on exceptional significance. When Beren and Lúthien enter Angband to recover a Silmaril from Morgoth's Iron Crown, their undertaking calls for courage, cunning and powers far beyond the abilities of ordinary mortals. Beren's deed is an extraordinarily daring act of clandestine recovery, without making him a Thief in the mechanical sense of MERP-RMU.

On a different scale, the character's decisions may have important consequences. A valuable object may prove dangerous, stolen information may expose innocent people, and an apparently legitimate mission may advance the designs of a corrupt patron.

The lure of profit is an obvious temptation, but the pursuit of recognition or the desire to demonstrate one's skill can be just as dangerous. A Burglar convinced that no place is beyond their reach may undertake missions whose consequences they can no longer properly judge.

The profession thus offers an opportunity to explore the responsibility that comes with using one's talents. Stealth shields the character from other people's eyes; it does not absolve them of responsibility for their decisions.

The Thief Through the Ages

The profession can be considered across the different Ages of Middle-earth, taking account of the forms of society and the traditions present in each period.

In the First Age, great fortresses, Elven kingdoms and the wars against Morgoth provide a setting for reconnaissance and infiltration missions. A character may seek to enter an enemy dwelling, recover an object or carry information between threatened communities. The exploits of Beren and Lúthien offer literary inspiration for such undertakings, while belonging to an exceptional order of power.

In the Second Age, the growth of Númenor and the settlements of Middle-earth encourages the rise of cities, warehouses and important trading networks. Political rivalries, precious objects and knowledge held in great houses offer numerous opportunities to specialists in intrusion. The growing influence of Sauron may also lead some characters to seek information within communities subject to his authority.

In the Third Age, the profession naturally finds a place in the cities of Gondor, the ports of Umbar, merchant communities and the ruins of ancient kingdoms. Bilbo Baggins is the most famous literary example of the Burglar, while the wars against Angmar and Sauron give clandestine missions particular importance.

In the Fourth Age, the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom and the renewal of exchanges between regions foster new commercial activities. Ancient structures can be explored, the roads grow busier again, and rivalries between families or communities provide varied reasons to employ the Thief's abilities. Some place their talents at the service of reconstruction and the recovery of lost possessions; others pursue undertakings whose legitimacy remains open to question.

Each period gives the character a different environment, where mechanisms, social rules and risks depend upon the history of the peoples concerned.

Leaving Familiar Streets

The Thief often practises their skills in places they know well. The habits of the inhabitants, lesser-known passages and familiar buildings are essential resources for their effectiveness.

Setting out on an adventure confronts them with environments where this knowledge is no longer enough. The great roads lead to regions whose customs are unknown to them, ruins contain unfamiliar mechanisms, and foreign communities react differently to their presence.

Some take the road to fulfil a particular mission. A patron asks them to recover an object, a relative has disappeared after a dangerous affair, or a former companion seeks their help in entering a guarded place.

Others wish to leave behind a life that has become too dangerous. A theft has drawn the attention of a powerful family, a mission has been compromised, or an old association now threatens the character's freedom.

Within a company, the Thief gradually discovers the value of their companions' abilities. The Ranger knows the passages through the wild, the Fighter offers protection, and the Alchemist can examine objects whose magical nature lies beyond the Thief's own knowledge.

In return, the Thief enables the group to approach difficulties that strength or magic might not necessarily resolve. They observe the surroundings, examine locking devices and suggest routes that sometimes avoid a confrontation.

These experiences change their habits. A character accustomed to working alone must learn to explain their decisions and accept that their companions share the risks they take.

Trust then becomes one of the greatest challenges in their life. It is built through journeys and promises kept, especially when their past remains unknown to those who travel beside them.

Playing a Thief

The Thief offers the opportunity to portray a character whose principal qualities are dexterity, observation and mastery of delicate situations.

A young Hobbit may have left the Shire after discovering an unexpected taste for adventure. A former locksmith's apprentice from Gondor uses the knowledge of her trade to work with investigators or merchant houses. A Dúnadan spy seeks the information needed to protect his people, while a burglar from Umbar has learned to survive amid the rivalries of the great families.

The character's training is an essential part of their history. Who taught them to understand locks? Were they trained by a craftsman or by a true burglar? Did their first mission end in a remarkable success, or do they still remember a companion arrested because of a mistake?

Their relationships with others also play an important role. A patron regularly entrusts them with delicate assignments; a family knows nothing of the true nature of their activities; a former associate knows a secret they wish to preserve.

Their personality may be shaped by years spent observing others. Some Thieves develop great patience, accustomed to waiting for hours until the right moment arrives. Others become particularly suspicious, especially after being betrayed by someone they trusted.

Success can also foster pride. A character who has opened several chests reputed to be impregnable may begin to regard every obstacle as a personal challenge. Conversely, one who has endured arrest or serious injury may become excessively cautious.

The profession is especially suited to campaigns centred on investigations, intrigue, travel and the exploration of ancient places. It allows for very different characters, from the professional burglar to the adventurer whose technical skills help keep their companions safe.

In the course of their life, the Thief will discover that the hardest doors to pass through do not always have locks. Earning the trust of others, remaining faithful to a promise and choosing to forgo a considerable profit may require more courage than entering a carefully guarded house.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Thief in MERP-RMU

The Thief, also known as the Burglar, is a non-spell user specialising in stealth, mechanisms, manipulation and movement.

Prime Stats

Their prime stats are Agility (Ag) and Quickness (Qu).

Agility represents the precision of movement and coordination necessary for manipulating mechanisms. Quickness supports movement, reactions and manoeuvres performed when the character must act under difficult conditions.

Skill Orientation

These skills must be developed in accordance with the mechanisms actually available in MERP-UI.

The choice of weapons and protection depends on the character's culture and history. Encumbrance, armour and movement restrictions remain those prescribed by RMU.

No Base Spell Lists

The Thief has no professional Base Spell Lists.

Any possible study of magic remains subject to the system's general rules and the limitations actually applied in MERP-RMU. Stealth, manipulation and infiltration abilities must not be treated as supernatural powers.

The Thief and the Rogue

The mechanical distinction remains important.

The Rogue enjoys training more evenly balanced between weapons and subterfuge skills. The Thief has particularly favourable costs in the Awareness, Subterfuge and Technical categories.

Faced with a complex lock, a concealed mechanism or an infiltration mission, the Thief is therefore the company's natural specialist, assuming comparable levels of skill development.

Both professions may nevertheless belong to the same cultures and undertake similar activities. Their main difference lies in their training.

Bilbo Baggins and the Burglar Tradition

Bilbo is a particularly apt literary reference for this profession, but his story remains unique.

He begins his journey without professional training as a burglar. His experience develops over the course of his adventures, while the Ring on certain occasions gives him a supernatural advantage that does not belong to the Thief's ordinary skills.

The Gamemaster may draw inspiration from his development to portray a character who gradually discovers their talents.

The extraordinary deeds of Beren and Lúthien, especially the recovery of a Silmaril from Angband, likewise belong to Tolkien's accounts, but must not be reduced directly to the Thief's ordinary game mechanics.

Shadow and Corruption

The profession has no inherent association with the Shadow.

The character's actions may nevertheless bring about the consequences prescribed by the Shadow and Corruption rules, notably when they willingly serve corrupted powers, betray their commitments or take part in acts of domination and cruelty.

Theft, stealth and intrusion must be judged according to their circumstances and intentions, without automatically treating the use of professional skills as a manifestation of Corruption.

The Thief comes fully into their own in MERP-RMU when their talents open new possibilities for the company and the decisions they make give real significance to their art.
